 Nearly 25 Million Older Medicare Beneficiaries Had Obesity in 2021 to 2023, More Than Double the 1999 Count
 Published Nov 15, 2026 11:38 PM EST 
 By
 Cole Mercer 
 Justin Sullivan | Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 About 24.6 million Medicare beneficiaries ages 65 and older had obesity in 2021 to 2023, up from 9.7 million in 1999 to 2000, according to an analysis of federal survey data presented at ObesityWeek 2026. The share of older beneficiaries with obesity climbed from 33.6% to 40.5% over that period, AJMC reported .
 Severe obesity, defined as a body mass index of 40 or higher, grew faster. It rose from 4.5% to 7.4% of older beneficiaries, or from about 1.3 million to 4.5 million people. The pace also picked up: the number of beneficiaries with obesity grew by about 0.54 million a year through 2013 to 2014, then by about 1.16 million a year after that, roughly double the earlier rate.
 The trend reaches households as well as Medicare's budget. Older adults with obesity in the study had far higher rates of diabetes, liver disease and heart failure, conditions that drive medication costs, doctor visits and the daily work of adult children who help care for aging parents.
 An Aging Population Meets Rising Rates
 Part of the jump reflects population growth. The number of Medicare beneficiaries 65 and older represented in the survey rose from 28.8 million to 60.9 million over the same period as baby boomers aged into the program. That means the number of people with obesity would have grown even if rates had held steady.
 But rates did not hold steady. Obesity prevalence rose by nearly 7 percentage points, and severe obesity by almost 3 points, so a larger share of older adults now live with the condition than two decades ago. The faster growth after 2013 to 2014 came as more baby boomers, who began turning 65 in 2011, entered Medicare, though AJMC's summary does not break down the causes.
 The analysis used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey , or NHANES, a federal survey that pairs interviews with physical exams. It included 14,916 adults 65 and older who reported having Medicare. The abstract's listed authors are P. Muntner, B.C. Jaeger, V. Bittner, and colleagues.
 Diabetes, Liver Disease and Heart Failure Far More Common
 In 2021 to 2023, 40.2% of older beneficiaries with obesity and 53% of those with severe obesity had diabetes, compared with 19.4% of those without obesity. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, an advanced form of fatty liver disease known as MASH, affected 17.4% and 21.4% of the two obesity groups, compared with 3.2% of those without obesity.
 Heart failure affected 11.4% of beneficiaries with obesity and 23.3% of those with severe obesity, versus 6.2% of those without obesity. High blood pressure and arthritis followed the same pattern.
 These are associations from a snapshot survey. They do not show that obesity caused each condition, and some people may have gained weight because arthritis or heart disease limited their mobility. Still, the gaps are large, and they show where the medical and financial burden is concentrated.
 Those facing the greatest burden include older adults with severe obesity, people already managing diabetes or heart failure, and those with limited mobility. Caregivers often feel the strain first, through more appointments, more prescriptions, and more help with daily tasks. Heart failure in particular can bring frequent medication changes, daily weight checks, and hospital stays, work that often falls to spouses or adult children.
 Limits of Self-Reported Survey Data
 Medicare status in NHANES is self-reported, so some participants may have misidentified their coverage. The survey is cross-sectional, meaning it captures different people at different points in time rather than following the same people. The findings come from a conference abstract that has not been published in a peer-reviewed journal, and AJMC's summary did not list the authors' institutions or funding. It also did not report results by race, income, or region, which could show where the burden is heaviest.
 BMI also has limits in older adults . It does not distinguish fat from muscle and can miss age-related muscle loss , so doctors often consider waist size, strength, and other measures alongside it.
 Coverage Options for Seniors and Caregivers
 Federal law bars Medicare Part D from covering drugs used only for weight loss. Since July 1, 2026, a temporary program called the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge has offered Wegovy and Zepbound for weight management to eligible Part D enrollees for a $50 monthly copay. The program runs outside the regular Part D benefit through December 2027. KFF estimated that about 3.8 million Part D enrollees would have met the eligibility criteria in 2023.
 The program has gaps. People who already filled a GLP-1 prescription under Part D in 2026 are not eligible, and neither are people with certain diagnoses, including type 2 diabetes, according to KFF. The copay does not count toward the Part D deductible or out-of-pocket cap, and the low-income subsidy does not apply. "For low- and modest-income individuals, the $50 copayment could be a barrier to participation ," KFF noted . People who take a GLP-1 under Part D for type 2 diabetes or another covered use keep getting it through their plan, even if that plan's cost-sharing is higher than $50.
 Medicare also covers intensive behavioral therapy for obesity for people with a BMI of 30 or higher, and bariatric surgery for some people with a BMI of 35 or higher and a related health condition. MedicalDaily previously explained who qualifies for the $50 GLP-1 program .
 Seniors and caregivers can ask a primary care doctor about screening for diabetes, fatty liver disease and heart failure, and whether weight treatment makes sense given muscle strength, fall risk and other medicines. Medicare open enrollment runs through Dec. 7, and Bridge access depends on having Part D coverage . Free, unbiased plan counseling is available through State Health Insurance Assistance Programs.
 The next steps are peer-reviewed publication of the analysis and federal data on how many beneficiaries use the Bridge program. MedicalDaily will report on both as they are released.

 Key Questions Answered
 How many older Medicare beneficiaries have obesity? About 24.6 million in 2021 to 2023, up from 9.7 million in 1999 to 2000, based on federal survey data.
 Is the increase only because there are more seniors? No. The older Medicare population roughly doubled, but the obesity rate also rose from 33.6% to 40.5%, and severe obesity rose from 4.5% to 7.4%.
 Which health problems were more common? Diabetes, fatty liver disease MASH, heart failure, high blood pressure, and arthritis were all more common among beneficiaries with obesity.
 What are the study's main limits? Medicare status was self-reported, the survey is a snapshot rather than a long-term study, and the findings have not been peer-reviewed.
 Does Medicare cover weight-loss drugs? A temporary program offers Wegovy and Zepbound for weight management to eligible Part D enrollees for $50 a month through December 2027.
 Where can families get help comparing coverage? State Health Insurance Assistance Programs offer free counseling, and Medicare open enrollment runs through Dec. 7.
